prime.problem: Before you can say how long a model step takes, you need to know how much work it is. Without a quick count you can't budget a training run, compare a dense model with an MoE, or notice that a chip with more FLOPs won't help decode.
prime.fits: Turns the forward-pass card's parameter count into work, and adds the attention card's context-dependent term. The machine half of the course then asks how long that work takes, and whether math is even the bottleneck.
prime.goal: Estimate FLOPs per token and a training run's total from a parameter count, say when the estimate goes wrong, and explain why a FLOP count alone can't predict decode speed.

attend: Why does one token through a matrix cost exactly twice that matrix's parameter count?
The matmul count comes to 93.5% of 2N. Which parameters are in N but do no multiplications?
Why does the backward pass cost about twice the forward, and what raises 6N to 8N?
Attention's q·Kᵀ and scores·V are matmuls too. Why doesn't 2N count them, and at what context do they matter?
At batch 1 the H100 finishes the math 295× sooner than the weights arrive. Why is that ratio a property of the chip rather than the model?

must: Every multiply is paired with an add → an (m×k)·(k×n) matmul costs 2mkn → one token (m = 1) through a matrix costs 2 × its parameters → a forward pass ≈ 2N FLOPs per token (16.06 GFLOP for Llama-3.1-8B)

Backward needs gradients for activations and for weights → about 2× the forward → training ≈ 6N per token and 6ND per run (7.23e23 for 8B on ~15T tokens) → recomputing activations adds one more forward → ≈ 8N
Attention multiplies activations (cached K, V), not parameters → its 4·S·D per layer per token is invisible to 2N → it grows with context: +27% at 8k, 4.3× at 128k, break-even near 8D = 32,768 tokens
FLOPs are a count, not a time → FLOPs ÷ FLOP/s is only the math floor → at batch 1 reading 16.06 GB takes 295× longer than 16.06 GFLOP of math → the FLOP count says almost nothing about decode speed
elevated: For MoE, N means active parameters → DeepSeek-V3 serves at 2 × 37B = 74 GFLOP per token, not 1,342 → but memory must still hold all 671B
The embedding lookup is a table read → its 525M parameters count in N but cost no FLOPs → why the exact count is 93.5% of 2N
reference: the 40% MFU assumption and the 0.51M H100-hour estimate
Meta's 1.46M GPU-hours and the 405B check (3.79e25 vs 3.8e25)
the T/(8D) shortcut's assumptions (F = 4D, plain MHA)

compress.prompt: Close the card and write the napkin in four lines: FLOPs per token to serve, per token to train, per training run, and the correction for long context. Then one sentence on why the count can't give you decode latency.
checklist: 2 FLOPs per parameter per token (multiply + add)
6 per token to train (backward ≈ 2× forward), 8 with full recompute; 6ND per run
attention adds 4·S·D per layer per token, growing with context
for MoE use active parameters for FLOPs, total for memory
FLOPs ÷ FLOP/s is a floor that ignores the bytes, which dominate decode

retrieve.q: Explain why one token through W_gate costs exactly 117.44 MFLOP, and how that one fact becomes the 2N rule for a whole model.
answer: W_gate has 4,096 × 14,336 = 58.72M parameters
each is multiplied once and added once for a one-row input: 2 × 58.72M
every matrix in the model works the same way, so a forward pass costs about 2 × (all parameters that do matmuls)

retrieve.q: Walk through the estimate of Llama 3.1 8B's pretraining compute and the H100-hours it implies at 40% MFU. What does the gap to Meta's 1.46M hours suggest?
answer: if all 1.46M hours were this one run, MFU would be only 13.9%
the card's unverified guess: the hours cover more than one clean pass, and small models reach lower MFU

retrieve.q: At what context length would you stop trusting 2N for Llama-3.1-8B, and what do you add instead?
answer: at 1k it's off by about 3%, at 8k by 27%
attention equals the matmuls near 8D = 32,768 tokens
add 32 × 4·S·4096 FLOPs per token (4.29 GFLOP at 8k); in a causal prefill, use about half of that

retrieve.q: DeepSeek-V3 has 671B parameters. What do you budget for FLOPs per token and for memory, and why are they different numbers?
answer: FLOPs: 2 × 37B active = 74 GFLOP per token
memory: all 671B, since any token may route to any expert
each token uses 8 of 256 routed experts plus 1 shared, so work follows active and storage follows total

compare.q: FLOP counting vs the roofline: what does the roofline add, which design choice in it fixes the FLOPs-only estimate, and where does each one fail?
answer: FLOP counting measures work; the roofline also counts bytes and takes the max of the two times
comparing intensity with the chip's ridge tells you which resource is the limit
FLOPs-only says a decode step takes 0.016 ms; the floor is 4.79 ms (about 300× off)
the roofline still ignores caches, launch overhead and imperfect overlap

compare.q: 2N per token vs the step-time formula: when is FLOPs ÷ FLOP/s a good estimate of a decode step, and when is it useless?
answer: step ≈ KV reads + max(weight reads, 2·B·N ÷ C)
the FLOP term only wins once the batch passes the critical batch size (≈ 295 on an H100 in BF16), or in prefill
at small batch the weight-read term wins and the FLOP count is irrelevant to latency

predict.q: Prefill one 131,072-token prompt through Llama-3.1-8B. Before computing: is the average compute per prompt token closer to 2N, to 5.3× 2N (the card's 128k row), or somewhere between?
predict.answer: In between, about 3.1× 2N. With the causal mask, token t only attends to t earlier tokens, so the prompt averages half the context: attention adds 68.72 ÷ 2 = 34.36 GFLOP per token on top of 16.06, giving about 50.4 GFLOP (computed). The 128k row is the cost of one decode token at the end of that context.

apply.task: By hand, fill a table for Llama-3.1-8B at contexts 1,024, 8,192, 32,768 and 131,072: attention FLOPs per token (32 × 4·S·4,096), total per token with 2N = 16.06 GFLOP, and attention's share of the total. Then set CONTEXT = 131072 in labs/flops-per-token.py to check your last row.
apply.done: Attention 0.54 / 4.29 / 17.18 / 68.72 GFLOP; totals 16.60 / 20.36 / 33.24 / 84.78 GFLOP; attention's share of the total 3.2% / 21.1% / 51.7% / 81.1% (computed).
apply.hint: Share of the total isn't the card's 'relative to 2N' column: divide attention by (2N + attention), not by 2N.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the causal halving, or where the 128k row applies?
Could you explain why the backward pass costs twice the forward without just quoting 6N?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: context → attention FLOPs, or FLOPs → time?
Did you mix up 'relative to 2N' and 'share of the total' in the table? That's the same slip a benchmark report can make.
What will you reopen before the GPU card: the 2mkn rule, or the 'same FLOPs, different hardware' table?
